content:
I have Claude and Aristotle working together an automated port of the 4-Color Theorem from Rocq .

Aristotle is an AI tool that runs in batch mode in the cloud. On my first attempt, I just gave the whole Rocq implementation to Aristotle and asked it to port it. It spent most of the day making a rough outline, then decided to stop.

Since then, I've written an MCP server for Claude to control Aristotle. MCP is just a way to give an LLM access to run external tools - in this case, the ability to run the aristotle command to submit work, check progress, and download results.

The general workflow is that Claude runs on a loop where every 15 minutes or so it checks whether Aristotle is done with its work, and if so, reviews and integrates the code, and then breaks of new pieces of the proof to assign.

This is a meant to be a straight port of Gronthier's earlier formalization, so hopefully it'll be a little nicer than some of the other AI proofs we've seen. (Or at least as "nice" as the 4ct proof can be...)

https://github.com/tangentstorm/fourcolor-lean?tab=readme-ov-file#readme
This topic was moved here from #Project announcements > Porting the 4-Color Theorem from Rocq by Patrick Massot.

I feel like the challenge here is not the translation of the math, but getting it to run fast enough. Isn’t the four color theorem mostly a big reduction in the kernel? Is Lean’s kernel fast enough for something similar?
Too early to tell. But yes, there's a huge pile of graphs that have to be individually validated. Gronthier Robin Thomas got the number down to 633 cases in 1998. Not sure what's changed since then.
I guess that ruins my plans to do a human formalization of this. Sad day.

But to validate them, you have to do a kernel reduction (i.e. rfl) or some tactic which does something similar. (I asked about how it works once here: https://proofassistants.stackexchange.com/questions/1105/how-does-the-formal-proof-of-the-four-color-theorem-work.) Anyway, good luck, but I'd be surprised if this was smooth.

Michal Wallace (tangentstorm) said:

why? It's already been formalized.

I could ask you the same question

I mean. It's a big chunk of tedious work that's been sitting there for years on the 100 proofs to-do list. I'd always thought about tackling it myself, and realized I'm probably never going to get past the "someday" stage. Then I discovered Aristotle and figured I'd try it out.
But I mean... Why does it ruin your plans? I get there's some kind of social credit/status for being the first to formalize something, but this has already been formalized for 20+ years.
But not in Lean / using Mathlib. The fact is that it does ruin them to me.

Hmm. Well, I think there will be tremendous opportunity for you (or anyone) to make improvements to whatever this thing comes up with. There's a reasonable chance this winds up being a disaster, and maybe simply observing what's terrible about it will help illuminate a better way?

Perhaps another set of agents should be set to analyze the current set of graphs, find commonalities, and optimize the procedure for length/brevity. Even noting that the procedure for graph X implies that for graph Y (where X is different from Y) would be a worthy contribution for publication as a note.

content:
Michal Wallace (tangentstorm) said:

I think there will be tremendous opportunity for you (or anyone) to make improvements to whatever this thing comes up with.

I can't speak for others, but I will not be engaging with this AI output.
Unless it miraculously spits out amazing mathlib-like code (which I think is more unlikely here than for other projects since the original code is very big).

Fair enough. I would imagine it's going to stick pretty close to translations of the individual Rocq statements, and of course that project wasn't based on anything resembling Mathlib.

My plan right now is to just let Claude and Aristotle work autonomously until the proof is completely ported and verified... And then start trying to read and understand it. Anything that isn't easy for me to understand is going to get rewritten and clarified until it is.

Most likely, though, it will still not be Mathlib quality just because I'm lacking quite a bit of mathematical background, and will probably wind up "dumbing things down" to my level. (Though hopefully I'll raise that level along the way...)

Michal Wallace (tangentstorm) said:

My plan right now is to just let Claude and Aristotle work autonomously until the proof is completely ported and verified... And then start trying to read and understand it.

Cf what happened with the autoformalised version of the sphere packing project

Anyway, if someone is looking for a similar, but yet unformalized (to the best of my knowledge) proof, they can formalize the minimal energy configuration of 5 points on a sphere, that is Thompson’s problem. https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.3702 Like the original Four Color and Kepler Conjecture proofs is it a yet unformalized computer proof (although in this case, there is a lot of interval arithmetic). https://arxiv.org/abs/1001.3702
BTW a quick literature search will reveal that more recent computer-assisted non-formal proofs have happened since 4CT was formalised. Eg https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-2010-05092-5

BTW a quick literature search will reveal that more recent computer-assisted non-formal proofs have happened since 4CT was formalised. Eg https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.0043 This one only uses so-called D-reducible graphs, at the cost of more than 633

Snir Broshi said:

I guess that ruins my plans to do a human formalization of this. Sad day.

Did you have a serious plan to do this? What is your estimate for the amount of (human) time required? (My rough guess has been 6 months FTE for someone with Lean experience, and a basic idea of the maths, e.g. has heard of discharging...)
But this (porting to Lean) has always struck me as a project that humans shouldn't do. There are just so many more interesting things for the time commitment.
(Separately, I don't understand the sentiment that a team involving AI, or solely AI, makes the result less interesting, but :woman_shrugging:.)

(Separately, separately, I'm very skeptical that in early 2026 someone who is not already expert in constructing efficient (i.e. efficiently kernel checkable) proofs in Lean has any chance of pointing some AIs at this and getting anywhere at all.)

You mean because they tend to set the max heartbeats to 800 trillion on every lemma? (and then use them up)

The first proofs I got back from Aristotle were like that, but I've found that if you just tell it to use simple tactics instead, it'll listen. (And it was able to clean up its messes after the fact as well.)

No, because naively generated proofs of the actual hard parts of 4CT might take the lifetime of the universe to check in the Lean kernel, which is designed for very different things than the Rocq kernel.
Ah. Good to know. I'll watch out for that. Thanks!

@Ian Allen

Well, it's known (I believe) that you can have just a set of "D-irreducible" configurations, which are apparently somehow "better" than needing to also include "C-reducible" ones, but you need more than 633, namely 2822 of them, according to https://arxiv.org/abs/0905.0043 (and the newer https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.24880 uses even more, including those 2822, to get a better asymptotic colouring algorithm)
